newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH TAX MOVE COULD TRIGGER WAVE OF DEMERGERS.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH TAX MOVE COULD TRIGGER WAVE OF DEMERGERS.

text.p: A recent Dutch government decision not to tax book profits on corporate demergers could prompt action by several companies currently dithering on whether to split themselves up, analysts believe.
A prime candidate to seek separate bourse listings for its main businesses is post and telecoms and giant Koninklijke PTT Nederland which is widely expected to announce a split-up later this year.
"KPN is a very clear example of how separate listings can add value," says Delta Lloyd analyst Peter Wortel.
"Its promising postal arm would then no longer be braked by price/earnings ratios which really apply to KPN's telecoms activities," he explains.
Patrick Wollenberg, telecoms analyst at IRIS Research, agrees the change in the law could facilitate a KPN split.
"This new legislation will certainly help rather than hinder a decision," he said.

Other candidates for a break-up in the longer term are electronics giant Philips and chemicals group Akzo Nobel, tipped by some to spin off its high-margin pharmaceuticals business as a separate entity.

Until now Dutch tax laws posed a disincentive to adding shareholder value in this way, as investors in firms listing their activities separately had to pay tax over the nominal value of the new shares they received in the spun-off entity.
This levy will be abolished under the new regime, set to take effect on January 1 next year.
For this reason retail and services concern Vendex said recently it planned to delay the allocation of shares in its newly-listed temporary employment arm Vedior to its shareholders until 1998.
Delta Lloyd's Wortel believes that now the tax measures have finally been approved, Vendex could list its remaining 80 percent Vedior stake earlier than originally planned.
Separate listings allow the individual businesses to be valued according to their real potential, analysts say.

"Vedior will be valued in line with high-performing temporary employment services stocks like Randstad , while Vendex will be ranked along with other retail stocks," said one analyst who asked not to be named.
While Vedior helped to lift Vendex's share price, the stock need not slide once Vedior is removed, because a return to core business is usually interpreted as positive, he adds.
"It's the classic situation of one plus one equals three -- or more," agrees Delta Lloyd's Wortel.
"What you often see in this kind of situation is that there's a holding company discount," says IRIS's Wollenberg. "The stock is marked down because it's a conglomerate."

According to Wollenberg's calculations, the combined value of the separately listed units of Dutch KPN would amount to some 80.50 guilders, five guilders more than the current 75.50 share price for the company as a whole.
While KPN is widely tipped as the next Dutch company to unbundle, some analysts are putting their money on a longer-term split up of Akzo Nobel and Philips.
"I think a spin-off of Akzo Nobel's pharmaceuticals activities is still a realistic option, although the company has ruled it out for the time being," says Patrick Rutten of Van Lanschot Bankiers.
A separate listing for pharmaceuticals would most probably go hand-in-hand with a takeover, he adds.
"A pharmaceuticals listing would achieve a far higher price/earnings ratio -- say 16 or 17 (times earnings) -- while the remaining activities would rate around 10 to 11," he says.

Higher per-share returns would facilitate a share offering to finance a takeover, although Akzo Nobel has a relatively low sensitivity to patents expiry -- the driving factor behind the recent wave of consolidation in the sector, Rutten believes.
Marina Millington-Ward, chemicals analyst with Bangert Pontier, rules out a short-term spin-off.
"It sounds like a good idea on paper, but I don't see it happening now or in the next few years," she says.
Philips could be a more likely candidate to unbundle with analysts suggesting separate listings for either its semiconductors or consumer electronics activities.
"Philips could spin off various parts, but you'd have to see what's left," says Wortel. "Semi-conductors might be a good bet to list separately."
However, in terms of adding shareholder value the electronics giant has already improved considerably under the stewardship of chairman Cor Boonstra, he adds.

Other companies which might do well to unbundle are food and drinks group BolsWessanen , whose merged activities never delivered the hoped-for synergies, and paper, packaging and office products group KNP BT where the highly cyclical paper business is proving a major headache.
But analysts generally agree that these firms will not take the separate listings route.

"For companies to list activities separately, both parts must be attractive," says Wortel. "Not only that, but both should have sufficient critical mass -- minimally they should qualify for the AMX (Amsterdam Midcap Index)."
As such BolsWessanen is likely to continue its gradual sell-off of its drinks activities, replacing them with food acquisitions.
KNP BT meanwhile had decided to seek a buyer for its Leykam paper unit.
Small and/or unprofitable, such activities could never make it as independently listed entities, analysts say.
